title: Advanced Patterns
subtitle: How big systems stay organized
description: As systems grow, you can't keep everything in one place. This module covers the architectural patterns that let large-scale applications stay manageable, responsive, and resilient.

lessons.title: Microservices vs. Monolith: One big app or many small ones?
lessons.description: The fundamental choice in how you structure your system — and why there's no universally right answer.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
When you build an app, all your code has to live somewhere. You have two broad options:

- A **[[glossary:monolith|monolith]]** is a single application that handles everything — user accounts, payments, notifications, search, all in one codebase and one deployment.
- **[[glossary:microservices|Microservices]]** split that single application into many small, independent services, each responsible for one thing. The user service handles users. The payment service handles payments. The notification service handles notifications.

Both approaches power real products at massive scale. Shopify runs a famously large monolith. Netflix runs famously many microservices. The choice isn't about which is "better" — it's about which tradeoffs make sense for your situation.

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
This is one of the most consequential architectural decisions a team makes, and it's hard to reverse. Understanding the tradeoffs helps you:

- **Evaluate engineering proposals** — when your team says "we need to break out a microservice," you'll know what that actually means in terms of complexity and operational cost.
- **Set realistic timelines** — microservices add coordination overhead. A feature that touches three services takes longer than one that lives in a single codebase.
- **Avoid premature complexity** — many startups adopt microservices too early and drown in operational overhead before they have the traffic to justify it.
- **Plan for growth** — at some point a monolith may become a bottleneck. Knowing when and why helps you plan the migration instead of panicking.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of it like food:

- A **monolith** is a food truck. One kitchen, one menu, one team. Everyone works side by side. Communication is easy — you just turn around and talk. Adding a new dish is simple because you have access to all the ingredients and equipment in one place. But if the fryer breaks, the whole truck shuts down. And as the menu grows, the kitchen gets cramped and chaotic.

- **Microservices** are a food court. Each stall is independent — the taco place, the pizza place, the sushi bar. Each has its own kitchen, its own staff, its own menu. If the pizza oven breaks, tacos and sushi keep flowing. But now you need a system to coordinate orders, each stall needs its own supplies, and adding a combo meal that spans three stalls requires careful coordination.

The food truck is simpler to run with a small team. The food court handles more variety and volume but needs more management overhead.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
**Start with a monolith** when:
- You're a small team (under 10-15 engineers)
- You're still figuring out your product and iterating quickly
- You don't yet have the operational maturity to manage distributed systems

**Consider microservices** when:
- Different parts of your system need to scale independently (your search feature needs 10x the resources of your settings page)
- Multiple teams are stepping on each other's toes in the same codebase
- A failure in one area (say, report generation) is crashing unrelated features (like user login)

Many successful companies start monolith and gradually extract services as they grow. That's not a failure — it's a strategy.

quiz.question: Monolith or microservices?
quiz.scenario: You're the PM at a 6-person startup that just raised a seed round. Your product is a project management tool with about 200 users. The CEO wants to "build it right from the start" and is pushing to adopt a microservices architecture with separate services for users, projects, notifications, and billing. Your sole backend engineer estimates this will add 3 months to the roadmap.

options.text: Go with the microservices plan — it's better to build the right architecture now than to rewrite later
options.explanation: With 6 people and 200 users, microservices would add significant operational overhead — managing multiple deployments, inter-service communication, distributed debugging — without any of the benefits. You don't have the team size or traffic to justify it, and those 3 months could be spent finding product-market fit.

options.text: Start with a monolith but keep the code well-organized so services can be extracted later if needed
options.explanation: A well-structured monolith gives you speed and simplicity now while keeping the door open for microservices later. With 200 users and a small team, your bottleneck is product iteration speed, not system architecture. Many billion-dollar companies ran monoliths well past this stage.

options.text: Compromise: build two services now (a main app and a billing service) and add more later
options.explanation: Even two services means your solo backend engineer now manages two deployments, inter-service networking, and distributed debugging. Billing at 200 users doesn't need its own service. This adds complexity without solving any actual problem you have today.

lessons.title: Message Queues: Not everything needs to happen right now
lessons.description: How systems handle work that can wait — and why trying to do everything instantly is a recipe for failure.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
A **[[glossary:message-queue|message queue]]** is a system that holds tasks in a line and processes them one at a time (or in batches), rather than handling everything the instant it arrives.

Here's the pattern:

1. Something happens in your app (a user places an order)
2. Instead of doing all the follow-up work immediately (charge the card, send confirmation email, update inventory, notify the warehouse), your app drops a message into a queue
3. Worker processes pick up messages from the queue and handle them

The user sees "Order confirmed!" in milliseconds. The email, inventory update, and warehouse notification happen seconds later in the background. The user never notices the delay, and your system stays fast.

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Message queues solve a set of problems that every growing system hits:

- **Speed** — users shouldn't wait for things they don't need to wait for. Sending a confirmation email takes 2 seconds, but the user doesn't need to stare at a spinner for it.
- **Reliability** — if the email service is down for 30 seconds, a queue holds the message and retries later. Without a queue, that email is lost.
- **Handling spikes** — if 10,000 people sign up in an hour during a launch, the queue absorbs the burst and your email service processes them at a steady pace instead of falling over.
- **Decoupling** — the part of your app that takes orders doesn't need to know anything about how emails are sent. It just puts a message in the queue and moves on.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of the order ticket system at a busy deli counter:

- You walk up, place your order, and get a ticket number. You're free to go sit down. That's the **producer** putting a message in the queue.
- Your order ticket goes on the rail behind the counter, joining a line of other orders. That's the **queue**.
- The kitchen staff work through the rail in order, making sandwiches one by one. They're the **consumers** (or workers).
- When your sandwich is ready, they call your number. That's the **callback** or result.

You didn't stand at the counter blocking everyone behind you while your sandwich was made. You got a fast acknowledgment (the ticket) and the actual work happened asynchronously.

Popular message queue tools include RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, and Redis (which can act as a simple queue). If you've used Zapier or background jobs in any app, you've used something similar.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Use a message queue when:

- **The user doesn't need the result immediately** — sending emails, generating reports, processing images, syncing data to analytics
- **Work can fail and needs retrying** — calling external APIs that might be temporarily down
- **You have traffic spikes** — a queue smooths out bursts so your downstream services don't collapse
- **You want to decouple services** — the order service shouldn't crash because the email service is having a bad day

You probably don't need a queue for:
- Simple apps with low traffic
- Operations where the user needs the result before they can continue (like checking if a username is available)

quiz.question: Should this be async?
quiz.scenario: Your e-commerce app has a checkout flow. When a user clicks "Place Order," your system needs to: (1) charge their credit card, (2) send a confirmation email, (3) generate a PDF invoice, and (4) notify the warehouse to ship. Currently all four steps happen synchronously, and users sometimes see a 12-second loading spinner at checkout. You've been asked to speed it up.

options.text: Put all four steps into a message queue so the user sees instant confirmation
options.explanation: You can't queue the credit card charge. The user needs to know immediately if their payment succeeded or failed — that's critical information that determines what happens next. If you queue it and the charge fails five minutes later, you've already told them the order is confirmed.

options.text: Charge the card synchronously, then queue the email, PDF, and warehouse notification
options.explanation: The credit card charge must happen in real time because the user needs to see success or failure immediately. But the email, invoice PDF, and warehouse notification can all happen in the background — the user doesn't need to wait for them. This cuts your checkout time from 12 seconds down to 2-3 seconds (just the payment processing).

options.text: Keep everything synchronous but add more server resources to handle it faster
options.explanation: Throwing more hardware at the problem might shave off a few seconds, but you're still making the user wait for work they don't need to wait for. The email and PDF will always take time regardless of server power, and external services like email providers have their own latency. The right fix is architectural: separate the must-wait work from the can-wait work.

lessons.title: Event-Driven Architecture: Services that react to what happens
lessons.description: Instead of services calling each other directly, they announce what happened and let others react.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
In a traditional system, services talk to each other directly. The order service calls the email service: "Send a confirmation email to this user." The order service calls the inventory service: "Decrease stock by one." The order service has to know about every other service and call each one.

In an **[[glossary:event-driven-architecture|event-driven architecture]]**, services don't call each other. Instead, they publish **events** — announcements that something happened. The order service says: "Hey everyone, an order was placed. Here are the details." Any service that cares about new orders can listen for that event and react on its own.

- The email service hears "order placed" and sends a confirmation
- The inventory service hears "order placed" and decreases stock
- The analytics service hears "order placed" and logs it

The order service doesn't know or care how many services are listening. It just announces what happened.

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Event-driven architecture matters because it changes how tightly your services are connected:

- **Adding features is easy** — want to add a loyalty points system? Just create a new service that listens for "order placed" events. You don't modify the order service at all.
- **Services are independent** — if the analytics service goes down, orders keep flowing. No one is waiting for analytics to respond.
- **Teams can work independently** — the email team doesn't need to coordinate with the order team. They just agree on the event format.
- **Audit trail for free** — since events are a record of everything that happened, you can replay them for debugging, auditing, or rebuilding data.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of a **newspaper subscription**:

- The **newspaper publisher** is like a service that produces events. Every morning, they print the paper and make it available. They don't know who reads it or what they do with it.
- **Subscribers** are like services that consume events. One subscriber reads the sports section. Another clips coupons. A third uses it for market research. Each subscriber independently decides what to do with the same newspaper.
- **Subscribing and unsubscribing** is trivial. A new reader can start getting the paper without the publisher changing anything. If someone cancels, the publisher doesn't notice.

Now compare this to the publisher personally calling every reader each morning and reading them the articles over the phone. That's the direct-call approach — it doesn't scale, and if one reader doesn't pick up, the publisher is stuck waiting.

Tools like Apache Kafka, Amazon SNS/EventBridge, and even simple webhook systems implement this pattern.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Event-driven architecture shines when:

- **Multiple services need to react to the same thing** — a new user signs up and you need to send a welcome email, create a default workspace, log it in analytics, and notify the sales team
- **You want loose coupling** — services should be able to evolve, deploy, and fail independently
- **You need an audit trail** — regulated industries (finance, healthcare) often require a complete record of every action
- **Your system is growing** — more teams, more services, more cross-cutting concerns

It may be overkill when:
- You have a small app with straightforward flows
- You need guaranteed ordering and immediate consistency (events are eventually consistent)
- Your team is small and the coordination overhead of event schemas isn't worth it yet

quiz.question: Direct calls or events?
quiz.scenario: Your ride-sharing app needs to handle what happens when a ride is completed. Currently, the ride service directly calls five other services in sequence: billing (charge the rider), payouts (pay the driver), ratings (prompt for a rating), analytics (log the ride), and receipts (email a receipt). Last week, the ratings service had a bug that caused the entire completion flow to fail — riders were charged but never got receipts.

options.text: Keep direct calls but add better error handling and retries to each call
options.explanation: Better error handling helps, but it doesn't fix the fundamental problem: the ride service is tightly coupled to five other services. Every new service that cares about ride completion means another direct call. And the ride service still has to know about and manage connections to all of them. You're patching symptoms instead of addressing the architecture.

options.text: Have the ride service publish a 'ride.completed' event and let each service react independently
options.explanation: With events, the ride service publishes one 'ride.completed' event and moves on. Billing, payouts, ratings, analytics, and receipts each listen independently. If ratings has a bug, it only affects ratings — billing and receipts keep working fine. Adding a new reaction (like a loyalty points service) means creating a new listener, with zero changes to the ride service.

options.text: Combine all five actions into the ride service itself so there are no external calls
options.explanation: This is the monolith approach — cramming everything into one service. It eliminates inter-service calls but creates a massive, unwieldy service responsible for billing, payouts, ratings, analytics, and receipts. Each of those domains has its own complexity and team. You'd lose the ability to deploy and scale them independently.

lessons.title: API Gateways: A single front door for your services
lessons.description: When you have many microservices, your clients need one place to talk to — not dozens.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
An **[[glossary:api-gateway|API gateway]]** is a single entry point that sits between your clients (web app, mobile app) and your backend services. Instead of your mobile app calling the user service, the order service, and the notification service directly, it calls one URL — the gateway — and the gateway routes the request to the right place.

The gateway handles the cross-cutting concerns that every request needs:

- **Routing** — directing `/users/me` to the user service and `/orders` to the order service
- **Authentication** — verifying the user's identity once, rather than in every service
- **Rate limiting** — preventing any single client from overwhelming your system
- **Response aggregation** — combining data from multiple services into one response so the client doesn't need to make five separate calls

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Without a gateway, every client needs to know about every service:

- Your mobile app calls `users.api.yourapp.com`, `orders.api.yourapp.com`, `notifications.api.yourapp.com` — and if you add or rename a service, you have to update every client.
- Every service has to implement its own authentication check, its own rate limiting, its own CORS headers.
- A single mobile screen that shows user info, recent orders, and notifications requires three separate API calls.

A gateway solves all of this by giving clients a single, stable interface. Behind that interface, you can restructure, split, merge, or replace services without clients ever knowing.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of a **hotel concierge**:

- You're the **guest** (the client). You want dinner reservations, theater tickets, and a car service. You could call three different places yourself, wait on hold, explain your preferences each time, and coordinate the timing.
- Or you tell the **concierge** (the API gateway) what you need. The concierge calls the restaurant, the theater, and the car service on your behalf, coordinates the timing, and comes back with one neat itinerary.
- The concierge also handles things you shouldn't have to think about — checking that you're actually a guest (authentication), making sure you're not booking 50 cars (rate limiting), and knowing which restaurant to call if your first choice is full (routing and fallback).

From your perspective, there's one person to talk to. Behind the scenes, the concierge manages all the complexity.

Popular API gateway tools include Kong, Amazon API Gateway, and nginx. Many teams use cloud platforms that include gateway functionality out of the box.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
You need an API gateway when:

- **You have multiple backend services** and clients shouldn't need to know about each one
- **You want centralized auth** — verify identity once at the gateway instead of in every service
- **Mobile apps need optimized calls** — aggregate data from multiple services into a single response to save battery and bandwidth
- **You need consistent rate limiting, logging, or monitoring** across all services

You probably don't need one when:
- You have a monolith (it already has one entry point)
- You have only two or three services and a small team — the overhead of managing a gateway might not be worth it yet
- Your app only has a web frontend that can easily call a few services directly

quiz.question: Where does the gateway help?
quiz.scenario: Your company's mobile app calls 8 different microservices directly. Users complain the app is slow and drains battery. Your mobile team says each screen makes 4-6 API calls to different services, and each call includes authentication logic. Meanwhile, your backend team just split the order service into two separate services, which will require a mobile app update to point to the new URLs.

options.text: Add an API gateway that aggregates calls and handles auth centrally
options.explanation: A gateway solves all three problems at once. It aggregates multiple backend calls into single responses (fewer round trips, less battery drain), centralizes authentication (removing duplicate logic from each service), and shields the mobile app from backend changes (the gateway URL stays the same even when services split or merge). The mobile app calls one endpoint per screen instead of 4-6.

options.text: Merge the microservices back into fewer, larger services to reduce the number of calls
options.explanation: Re-merging services throws away the benefits of having them separated (independent scaling, independent deployments, team autonomy). The problem isn't that you have too many services — it's that clients are directly coupled to all of them. A gateway lets you keep the backend architecture while simplifying the client experience.

options.text: Cache API responses on the mobile device so it makes fewer calls
options.explanation: Client-side caching helps with repeat requests but doesn't solve the core problems. The first load still requires 4-6 calls per screen. Auth logic is still duplicated everywhere. And the backend service split still breaks the app. Caching is a useful optimization but it doesn't address the architectural issue.

lessons.title: Webhooks: How apps notify each other when something happens
lessons.description: A pattern where one service calls your URL when an event occurs, instead of you constantly checking.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
A **webhook** is a URL that one service calls when an event happens. Instead of your app constantly asking another service "Any updates? Any updates? Any updates?" (that's called **polling**), you give the other service your URL and say, "Call me when something happens."

The pattern works like this:

1. You **register a webhook URL** with the external service (e.g., `https://yourapp.com/webhooks/stripe`)
2. When an event occurs (a payment succeeds, a form is submitted, code is pushed), the service sends a **POST request** to your URL with the event data
3. Your server receives the request, processes the event, and responds with a `200 OK` to acknowledge receipt

You've encountered webhooks if you've used:
- **Stripe** — sends a webhook when a payment succeeds, fails, or is refunded
- **GitHub** — sends a webhook when code is pushed, a PR is opened, or an issue is created
- **Shopify** — sends a webhook when an order is placed, a product is updated, or a customer signs up

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Webhooks enable real-time integrations without the waste of constant polling:

- **Efficiency** — polling means your app checks for updates every few seconds, even when nothing has changed. That's thousands of unnecessary [[glossary:api|API]] calls per day. Webhooks flip the model: zero traffic when nothing happens, one call exactly when something does.
- **Real-time** — with polling, there's always a delay (however often you check). Webhooks notify you the moment an event occurs.
- **Simplicity** — your app doesn't need to manage polling intervals, track what it's already seen, or handle "no new data" responses. It just receives events as they come.
- **Integration backbone** — webhooks are how most SaaS products connect to each other. They're the foundation of automation platforms like Zapier, Make, and IFTTT. When you set up a "when X happens in Slack, do Y in Google Sheets" automation, webhooks are the mechanism.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of it like **giving a restaurant your phone number** when the wait is long:

- **Polling** is calling the restaurant every 5 minutes: "Is my table ready yet?" "No." "Is my table ready yet?" "No." "Is my table ready yet?" It wastes your time, annoys the host, and you still don't get your table any faster.
- **A webhook** is giving them your number and saying, "Call me when it's ready." You go about your day. When the table is available, they call you once. You show up immediately.

The restaurant (the external service) does the notifying. You (your app) just need to be reachable at the number you gave them (your webhook URL).

In practice, implementing a webhook receiver involves:

1. **Create an endpoint** on your server (e.g., `/webhooks/stripe`) that accepts POST requests
2. **Register that URL** with the external service through their dashboard or API
3. **Parse the incoming data** — webhook payloads are usually JSON containing event type and relevant details
4. **Verify the signature** — most services sign their webhook payloads with a secret key so you can confirm it's really from them and not an attacker
5. **Respond with 200 quickly** — acknowledge receipt first, then process the event asynchronously. If your endpoint is slow to respond, the service may retry or assume it failed
6. **Handle retries** — if your endpoint is temporarily down, most services will retry several times with increasing delays. Design your handler to be **idempotent** (processing the same event twice produces the same result).

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Use webhooks when:

- **Receiving events from third-party services** — payment confirmations from Stripe, deployment notifications from GitHub, form submissions from Typeform. This is the most common use case.
- **Connecting your own [[glossary:microservices|microservices]]** — your order service can send a webhook to your fulfillment service when an order is placed, keeping them loosely coupled.
- **Building integrations and automations** — Zapier-style workflows are built on webhooks. "When a new row is added to this spreadsheet, create a task in the project tracker."
- **Real-time notifications** — instead of checking for new messages every second, let the messaging service tell you when one arrives.

Webhooks are less ideal when:

- **You need guaranteed delivery** — webhooks can be missed if your server is down. For critical events, pair them with a polling fallback or use a [[glossary:message-queue|message queue]] for guaranteed delivery.
- **You need to pull large datasets** — webhooks are for event notifications, not data transfers. If you need to sync thousands of records, use a batch API instead.
- **The source doesn't support them** — not every API offers webhooks. In that case, polling is your only option.

quiz.question: Which approach fits this integration?
quiz.scenario: Your app uses Stripe for payments. When a subscription payment fails (like an expired credit card), you need to immediately email the customer, pause their premium features, and log the event for your finance team. Currently, your app polls the Stripe API every 10 minutes to check for failed payments.

options.text: Switch to Stripe webhooks so you're notified immediately when a payment fails
options.explanation: Webhooks are the right fit here. Stripe sends a webhook the moment a payment fails, so you can email the customer, pause features, and log the event in near real-time. Polling every 10 minutes means a customer could use premium features for up to 10 minutes after their payment failed, your email notification is delayed, and you're making thousands of unnecessary API calls per day checking for events that haven't happened. Stripe's documentation explicitly recommends webhooks over polling for payment events.

options.text: Increase polling frequency to every 30 seconds for faster detection
options.explanation: Polling every 30 seconds is 2,880 API calls per day instead of 144, and you're still up to 30 seconds behind. Most of those calls return nothing new. You'd also risk hitting Stripe's rate limits. Webhooks eliminate all of this: zero calls when nothing happens, instant notification when something does. Polling harder is the brute-force approach when a more elegant solution exists.

options.text: Check payment status only when the user tries to access a premium feature
options.explanation: This is lazy evaluation, and it creates a bad user experience. The customer doesn't find out their payment failed until they try to use a feature and are suddenly blocked. They never got an email warning. Your finance team has no real-time visibility. And if the customer doesn't log in for a week, you've been providing premium service for free. Proactive notification via webhooks is the standard approach for payment status changes.

lessons.title: Task Scheduling: Running work on a clock, not on demand
lessons.description: Running work on a timer instead of on demand.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
A **scheduled task** (or **cron job**) is work that runs automatically at a set time or interval — not triggered by a user action, but by the clock. Examples:

- Sending a daily digest email at 8 AM
- Generating weekly analytics reports every Monday
- Cleaning up expired sessions every hour
- Checking for abandoned carts every 15 minutes and sending reminder emails
- Syncing data from an external [[glossary:api|API]] every 5 minutes

This is different from [[glossary:message-queue|message queues]] (event-triggered: "a user placed an order, process it") — scheduled tasks are time-triggered ("it's 8 AM, send the digest").

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Almost every production app has background work that needs to happen on a schedule. Understanding task scheduling helps you:

- **Scope features that involve periodic work** — daily reports, weekly summaries, recurring billing. These all need scheduling infrastructure, and that affects timelines.
- **Understand why "just run it every minute" isn't always simple at scale** — what if the task takes longer than the interval? What if two [[glossary:server|servers]] both try to run it?
- **Debug issues where scheduled work isn't happening** — "the daily report didn't go out" is a common support escalation that's hard to troubleshoot without understanding how scheduling works.
- **Plan infrastructure needs** for compute-intensive periodic work (like nightly data aggregation that processes millions of rows).

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Think of a **sprinkler system on a timer**:

You don't stand outside every morning and manually water the lawn. You set the sprinkler to run at 6 AM for 20 minutes. It runs automatically, rain or shine.

But what happens if the water pressure is low and it takes 40 minutes instead of 20? The next cycle might start before the first one finishes — that's a real problem in task scheduling called **overlapping runs**.

In practice, simple scheduled tasks use **cron** — a Unix utility where you define a schedule like "every day at midnight" or "every 5 minutes." Cloud platforms offer managed versions: AWS EventBridge Scheduler, Vercel Cron Jobs, Railway Cron.

For distributed systems (multiple [[glossary:server|servers]]), you need to ensure only one server runs the task — this uses a **distributed lock** (a flag in [[glossary:redis|Redis]] or the [[glossary:database|database]] that says "I'm already running this, don't start another"). Without a lock, every server runs the task independently, and your users get duplicate emails or corrupted data.

More complex scheduling needs tools like Temporal or BullMQ, which add features like retries, monitoring, and job history.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Use scheduled tasks for:

- **Periodic reports and summaries** — daily digests, weekly analytics, monthly invoices
- **Recurring billing and subscription management** — charging customers on their renewal date
- **Data cleanup and maintenance** — expiring old sessions, removing temporary files, archiving old records
- **Syncing data between systems** on an interval — pulling data from a third-party API every few minutes
- **Health checks and heartbeats** — verifying that external services are still responding

Use [[glossary:message-queue|message queues]] instead when:

- The work is triggered by an event, not a timer
- You need immediate processing
- The volume is unpredictable and bursty

quiz.question: Why are users getting duplicate emails?
quiz.scenario: Your SaaS app sends a "Weekly Activity Summary" email every Monday at 9 AM. It works perfectly in staging. In production with 3 servers behind a load balancer, users report receiving 3 copies of the summary email every Monday. The cron job is configured on each server.

options.text: All 3 servers are running the same cron job independently — you need a distributed lock or a single dedicated scheduler
options.explanation: All 3 servers are running the same cron job independently, so the task executes 3 times. You need either a distributed lock (so only one server acquires the lock and runs it) or move the cron job to a single dedicated worker/scheduler service. This is a classic distributed scheduling problem — it works in staging because staging typically runs on one server.

options.text: The load balancer is duplicating the cron job requests — configure it to route scheduled tasks to one server
options.explanation: Load balancers route incoming HTTP requests — they don't have anything to do with cron jobs. Cron runs locally on each server based on its own clock. The load balancer doesn't know the cron job exists and can't prevent it from running. The fix needs to happen at the scheduling layer, not the networking layer.

options.text: The email service is retrying failed sends — add deduplication logic to the email sending code
options.explanation: If the email service were retrying, you'd see inconsistent duplicate counts (sometimes 2, sometimes 4). Users are consistently getting exactly 3 copies — one from each server. The problem is that the task runs 3 times, not that a single run sends multiple emails. Deduplication could mask the symptom, but the real fix is ensuring the task only runs once.

lessons.title: Pub-Sub: Broadcasting events to anyone who's listening
lessons.description: A messaging pattern where publishers broadcast to a topic and any number of subscribers receive every message -- unlike queues, where each message goes to one worker.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
**Pub-Sub** (Publish-Subscribe) is a messaging pattern where senders (publishers) broadcast messages to a **topic**, and any number of receivers (subscribers) can listen to that topic. The publisher doesn't know who's subscribed. Subscribers don't know who published. The topic is the intermediary.

This is different from a [[glossary:message-queue|message queue]] where each message is consumed by ONE worker. In pub-sub, each message is delivered to ALL subscribers. If 5 services subscribe to the "order.placed" topic, all 5 get a copy of every message.

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Pub-sub matters because it's the backbone of [[glossary:event-driven-architecture|event-driven systems]] at scale. It enables:

- **Fan-out** -- one event triggers many reactions across different services
- **Decoupled services** -- publishers and subscribers evolve independently
- **Real-time features** -- push notifications, live updates, chat
- **Reliable delivery** -- messages persist in the topic even if a subscriber is temporarily down

Understanding the difference between queues and pub-sub helps you scope features correctly -- "notify all subscribers" is pub-sub, "assign this task to one worker" is a queue.

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Analogy: a **podcast**.

The host (publisher) records an episode and uploads it to a platform (topic). Every subscriber automatically gets the episode. The host doesn't know how many listeners they have or what they do with the episode -- one person listens while running, another takes notes, a third shares clips on social media. New subscribers can join anytime without the host changing anything. If a subscriber's phone is offline, they get the episode when they reconnect.

Compare this to a **phone call** (direct messaging) where you speak to ONE person and have to call each person individually. Or a **voicemail queue** where the first person to check it "consumes" the message. Pub-sub delivers to everyone.

Popular tools: Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Amazon SNS, Apache Kafka (which can act as both a queue and pub-sub), Redis Pub/Sub (simpler, no persistence).

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Use pub-sub when:

- One event needs to trigger actions in multiple independent services
- You need to broadcast updates (price changes, config updates, notifications)
- You're building real-time features (live feeds, collaborative editing, notifications)
- You want an audit log of all events

Use a regular [[glossary:message-queue|message queue]] instead when:

- Each task should be processed by exactly one worker (like sending an individual email or processing a single payment)

quiz.question: What pattern should you adopt?
quiz.scenario: Your e-commerce platform needs to handle what happens when a product's price changes. Currently, the pricing service directly calls the search index, the recommendation engine, the email notification service (to alert users watching the product), and the analytics service. Adding a new price comparison feature requires modifying the pricing service to also call the new comparison service. Your team is tired of updating the pricing service every time a new consumer of price data appears.

options.text: Have the pricing service publish a "price.changed" event to a pub-sub topic, and let each service subscribe independently
options.explanation: Each service (search, recommendations, email, analytics, comparison) subscribes to the "price.changed" topic independently. Adding the next consumer is zero changes to the pricing service. The pricing service just announces what happened; it doesn't need to know or care who's listening.

options.text: Create a shared library that the pricing service uses to call all consumers, so adding a new one is just a config change
options.explanation: A shared library still means the pricing service is responsible for calling every consumer. Even if adding a consumer is a config change, the pricing service still has to deploy that config, manage connections to each consumer, and handle failures in each one. You've made the coupling slightly more convenient but haven't eliminated it.

options.text: Put price changes into a message queue and have each service poll the queue for updates
options.explanation: A standard message queue delivers each message to ONE consumer. If the search service picks up a price change message, the recommendation engine never sees it. You'd need a separate queue for each consumer, which recreates the original problem of managing individual connections. Pub-sub's fan-out delivers every message to all subscribers automatically.

lessons.title: Payment Systems: How money actually moves through your app
lessons.description: The multi-step process behind every checkout -- authorization, capture, settlement -- and why idempotency keys prevent double charges.

sections.heading: what
sections.content:
Payment processing seems simple -- user clicks "Pay," money moves. In reality, it's a multi-step process with strict rules. The key stages:

- **Authorization** -- checking if the card is valid and has funds. No money moves yet.
- **Capture** -- actually charging the card. Money moves.
- **Settlement** -- the money arriving in your bank account, usually 2-3 business days later.

Many apps separate authorization and capture: a hotel authorizes $500 when you check in but only captures the actual total when you check out.

The critical concept is **idempotency** -- ensuring that if something goes wrong and a request is retried, the customer isn't charged twice. Payment processors like Stripe handle this with **idempotency keys**: a unique ID you send with each charge request so the processor knows "I already processed this one, don't charge again."

sections.heading: why
sections.content:
Payments are one of the highest-stakes features in any app. Getting it wrong means:

- **Charging customers twice** -- refund + angry user + potential chargeback fees
- **Not charging at all** -- lost revenue
- **Falling out of PCI compliance** -- legal consequences

Understanding payment flows helps you:

- **Scope checkout features realistically** -- it's never "just add a pay button"
- **Understand why payment features take longer to build than expected**
- **Debug payment issues** -- "the charge was authorized but never captured"
- **Evaluate payment providers** -- Stripe, Square, Adyen

sections.heading: how
sections.content:
Analogy: **buying a house**.

You don't hand over a suitcase of cash. First, the bank verifies you have the funds and issues a pre-approval (authorization). Then at closing, the actual money transfer happens (capture). Days later, the funds arrive in the seller's account (settlement). If the deal falls through after pre-approval, no money moved -- the authorization is simply voided.

In a typical Stripe integration:

1. User enters card details (handled by Stripe's UI component -- you never see the card number)
2. Stripe creates a PaymentIntent (authorization)
3. If the charge is confirmed, Stripe captures the funds
4. Stripe sends a **webhook** to your [[glossary:server|server]] confirming success
5. Your app fulfills the order

The webhook pattern is critical -- never rely on the client to confirm payment. A user could close their browser mid-checkout. The webhook from Stripe is the source of truth.

sections.heading: when
sections.content:
Use a managed payment processor (Stripe, Square) for almost everything -- never build payment processing yourself.

Think about payment edge cases when scoping:

- Refunds and partial refunds
- Subscription billing and failed renewals
- Currency conversion for international users
- Authorization holds vs. immediate charges
- Handling disputed charges (chargebacks)

These edge cases typically take 3-5x longer than the "happy path" checkout flow.

quiz.question: How do you prevent the double charges?
quiz.scenario: Your app charges users when they place an order. Occasionally, users report being charged twice for a single order. Your engineering team investigates and finds that sometimes the network times out after sending the charge request to Stripe, so the app retries the request -- which creates a second charge. The order itself is only created once.

options.text: Add an idempotency key (like the order ID) to every Stripe charge request so retries don't create duplicate charges
options.explanation: If the same idempotency key is sent twice, Stripe recognizes it as a retry and returns the original result instead of processing a new charge. This is the standard pattern for preventing duplicate payments. Using the order ID as the key is natural since each order should only be charged once.

options.text: Check if the order has already been charged before sending the request to Stripe
options.explanation: This creates a race condition. The first request times out -- your app doesn't know if Stripe processed it or not. Checking your own database won't tell you what Stripe did. You might see "not charged" in your database while Stripe actually did charge the card. The idempotency key solves this at the Stripe level, where the truth about the charge lives.

options.text: Increase the network timeout so requests don't time out in the first place
options.explanation: Longer timeouts reduce the frequency of the problem but don't eliminate it. Networks are unreliable -- timeouts, dropped connections, and server errors will always happen eventually. The idempotency key is the correct solution because it makes retries safe regardless of why they happen. You need a system that handles failure gracefully, not one that assumes failure won't occur.
